warehouses.title: Inventory 1 — Warehouses & the Stock Architecture
warehouses.desc: The foundation of the inventory certification: the warehouse as an accountability unit, tree design, the append-only stock ledger, the four numbers of a bin, the logical rooms, stock as custody of value, and the defaults that wire documents to the tree.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — What a warehouse is (and is not)
lessons.html:
Welcome to the third certification. Selling taught money-in; Procurement taught money-out; this track teaches the thing both of them move: stock — where it sits, how it moves, what it is worth, and who answers for it. And it begins where stock begins: the warehouse.

A warehouse is a named place stock can be. Not necessarily a building: the system's warehouse is an ACCOUNTABILITY unit — a distinct place with a distinct answer to what is here and who answers for it. A physical store is a warehouse; so is the quarantine bay inside it, the van doing branch deliveries, the goods sitting in transit between two branches, and the stock at your repacker's site that never stopped being yours. One building can hold several warehouses; one warehouse (the van, the transit) can have no building at all. The test is never architecture; it is custody: where a distinct accountability exists, a distinct warehouse names it — the principle this whole module unpacks.

Two kinds of node. Warehouses live in a TREE: leaf warehouses actually hold stock — every stock movement names a leaf; group warehouses hold structure — they aggregate their children for reporting and hold nothing themselves. Lagos Region is a group; Ikeja Branch Store is a leaf. Trying to move stock into a group node fails by design, and the refusal is teaching you the model: stock exists in PLACES; groups exist so places can be READ together.

The warehouse carries money. Every warehouse's stock has a value (Chapter 6 makes this operational), and in the books each warehouse's holdings roll into the firm's stock asset. This is why warehouse design is never merely logistics: creating a warehouse creates a bucket of company value with a custodian's name implicitly on it, and deleting, merging, or misusing warehouses moves the accounting ground under the operation.

What the item knew, the warehouse localises. Buying 2 built the item — one identity, one UOM discipline, one cost story. The warehouse dimension crosses it: every stock fact in this system is an item-AT-warehouse fact. PARA-500 does not have a quantity; it has a quantity AT Central, AT Ibadan, AT Quarantine, AT In-Transit — and the sum is the firm's position while the parts are the operation's truth. Every screen, report, and document in this track reads or writes that two-dimensional grid, and holding the grid in your head — items down, warehouses across — is the single mental model that makes the rest of the curriculum easy.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Designing the tree
lessons.html:
The warehouse tree is designed once and lived with for years, which makes its design hour the same kind of hour as the settings walk: the consultant writing a constitution. The principles, in the order to apply them.

Start from accountability, not architecture. List the distinct custodies the client actually runs: the central store, each branch's stock room, the quarantine bay, goods-in-transit between locations, the facilities/consumables store, any supplier-side stock (the subcontractor holding your materials), returns staging where returns are triaged. Each distinct custody becomes a leaf. What does NOT become a warehouse: shelf positions, aisles, and fridges inside one custody — that is bin-level detail, and modelling every shelf as a warehouse (the sprawl disease, Chapter 9) drowns the tree in places nobody separately answers for. The line to hold: would a stock difference here be a different PERSON'S problem? Yes — warehouse. No — location detail within one.

Shape the tree for reading. Groups exist for rollups, so group by how the firm asks questions: All Warehouses → Branches (group) → each branch leaf; Central operations grouped with their logical rooms; regions as intermediate groups only when the firm genuinely reads by region. Depth discipline: two or three levels serve almost every trading firm — a five-level tree is bureaucracy nobody navigates. The tree can be re-shaped later (groups re-parented) far more easily than leaves can be merged, so err simple.

Name for the decade. Names appear on every document, filter, and report forever: short, unambiguous, consistently patterned — the branch name leading (Ikeja Store, Ikeja Quarantine) so sorted lists group naturally, and no cleverness that needs explaining to the third cohort of staff. Where branches are companies-within-the-company (separate accountability entirely), the design conversation escalates beyond warehouses — flag it, don't improvise it.

One custody, one leaf — both directions. Every physical custody has exactly one system twin, and every system leaf means one real custody. The diseases are symmetrical: the physical room with no system warehouse (its stock booked into a neighbour, its differences invisible — the storeroom that exists in the building and not in the books); and the system warehouse with no physical meaning (created for a forgotten reason, accumulating misc postings — a junk drawer with a naira value). The annual tree review (this track's calendar will own it) walks both lists.

Defaults finish the design. A tree is used by documents, and documents choose warehouses by DEFAULTS (Chapter 7): the design is complete only when every routine flow lands in the right leaf without a human choosing — because the human, at speed, chooses wrong, and the wrong-warehouse posting is this track's most routine support ticket. Design the tree, then wire the defaults, then watch the first week's postings: the three steps of a warehouse implementation, in order.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The stock ledger: the append-only book
lessons.html:
Underneath every screen in this track sits one structure, and understanding it makes everything else transparent: the stock ledger — the append-only book of every stock movement the firm has ever made.

What an entry is. Every time stock moves, the ledger gains a dated line: item, warehouse, quantity in or out, the running balance after, the valuation effect (Chapter 6 and module 5), and — decisively — which document caused it. A receipt writes IN lines; a delivery writes OUT lines; a transfer writes an OUT at source and an IN at destination; a reconciliation writes the adjusting difference. The ledger is written ONLY by documents: no screen edits it directly, no administrator pencils a balance, and this is not a limitation but the entire design — the ledger is the firm's stock testimony, and testimony that can be quietly rewritten proves nothing.

Append-only, permanently. Corrections do not erase; they append. The wrong entry stands, and the correcting entry stands beside it, dated, attributed, explained by its own document — the same immutability doctrine both money tracks taught (the invoice never edited, the credit note appended), because it is the same ledger philosophy applied to goods. When a client asks can we just fix the number, the consultant's answer is this chapter: the number is a running balance COMPUTED from history; fixing it means appending the movement that makes history true (usually a reconciliation — module 4), never editing history to match a wish.

The bin: the ledger, summarised. For each item-at-warehouse, the system maintains the current position — the running totals the ledger implies: actual quantity, plus the promised dimensions (Chapter 4). Reading a bin is reading the ledger's last line; reading the LEDGER is reading how it got there — and the second read is the diagnostic superpower: any surprising balance decomposes into its history, entry by entry, document by document, until the surprise has a name (the transfer that never completed, the receipt posted to the wrong branch, the delivery that went out twice). Consultants who reach for the ledger first resolve in minutes what screen-starers escalate.

Chronology is load-bearing. Entries carry posting date and time, and the ledger is a TIMELINE: stock-as-at-a-date, valuation at each moment, and every dispute's evidence all read it in order. Backdating a movement rewrites every balance after it — sometimes legitimately (the receipt entered a day late, policy-governed), always consequentially (module 5 walks the valuation ripple). The gate disciplines both trading tracks taught (post at the event, never batch Friday into Monday) were protecting THIS structure; now you can see what they protect.

The auditor's favourite table. Everything this track will do — counts, valuations, branch networks, health reports — is a conversation with this ledger. The firm whose people understand that stops arguing with screens and starts reading history; and the audit, internal or external, that can walk any balance back to documents is the audit that ends early. One book, appended forever, written only by documents: hold that sentence; the track is its elaboration.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The four numbers of a bin
lessons.html:
Both trading tracks used the projected-stock arithmetic; this chapter makes you its owner. For every item-at-warehouse, four numbers describe the position, and reading them together is the warehouse professional's core literacy.

  • Actual — what the ledger says is physically here now: the sum of every in minus every out. The number a count would verify (module 4 tests it), the number custody answers for.
  • Reserved — what is promised OUT: submitted sales orders' undelivered quantities holding their claim (Selling 4's machinery). Physically present, commercially spoken for — sellable to no one else.
  • Incoming — what is promised IN: submitted purchase orders' unreceived quantities (Procurement 5's machinery), plus inbound transfers en route. Not here yet, but coverage the planners may count.
  • Projected = actual − reserved + incoming — the number decisions read: what will be here when promises keep. Reorder triggers watch it (Procurement 3), sales availability reads it (Selling 4), and planning plans it.

Reading a bin like a professional. The four numbers are a diagnosis in one row. Actual 500, reserved 480, projected 20: the shelf looks full and the branch is nearly sold out — the picker sees boxes, the system sees promises, and the system is right. Actual 40, incoming 300, projected 340: thin shelf, healthy position — panic buying now duplicates the Emzor order already coming. Actual 200, reserved 0, incoming 0, and no movement for months: the dead-stock read (module 7 prices it). The literacy is refusing to read ACTUAL alone — every actual-only decision (the sale promised off the visible shelf, the purchase panicked off the visible gap) is a decision made with a quarter of the information.

Where the promises live. Reserved and incoming are not typed anywhere — they are COMPUTED from open documents, which is why both trading tracks' hygiene rules were really inventory rules: the ghost reservation (the stale sales order hiding sellable stock) corrupts RESERVED; the phantom incoming (the stale purchase order promising goods forever) corrupts INCOMING; and both corrupt PROJECTED, the number everything downstream trusts. The sweeps those tracks installed are, from this track's chair, ledger hygiene — and the warehouse team has standing to demand them, because the warehouse inherits every planning error the corrupted number causes.

Per-warehouse, then rolled. Each number is item-AT-warehouse; the firm-level view sums the leaves — and the difference matters operationally: the firm may hold plenty while Ibadan holds none (a TRANSFER problem, not a purchase problem — module 6's terrain), and projected-at-Central answers a different question from projected-everywhere. The grid again: read the cell for operations, the rollup for strategy, and never confuse the two.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The logical rooms
lessons.html:
The tree's most powerful idea is the warehouse with no walls: the logical room — a leaf that names a custody state rather than a building. You have met every one of them in the earlier tracks; this chapter assembles them as a family and gives the design rule they share.

  • Quarantine (Procurement 6's rejected warehouse): stock in your possession but out of your sellable truth — damaged arrivals, failed inspections, short-dated rejections awaiting their fate. Its balance is a to-do list with a value; its weekly review is already on the procurement calendar.
  • In-transit: stock between two of your own custodies — on the truck from Central to Ibadan, owned by the firm and held by nobody's shelf. The two-step transfer (module 2 runs its mechanics, module 6 its governance) parks the goods here between dispatch and receipt, so at every moment SOMETHING answers for them: the sender no longer, the receiver not yet, the transit room precisely. Its balance is the network's bloodstream, and its AGING is the network's diagnostic — transit stock older than any truck journey is a truck that never arrived, a receipt never confirmed, or a leak (module 6 owns the discipline).
  • Supplier-side / subcontract stock (Procurement 8): your materials at their site — ownership retained, location external, exposure visible as a balance instead of a hope.
  • Returns staging: customer returns landing for triage before their fate (restock, quarantine, write-off — Selling 5's fork needs a floor to stand on). A distinct room where the firm's return volume justifies distinct accountability; folded into quarantine where it does not.
  • The facilities/consumables store: not glamorous, but internal consumption (Procurement 3's Material Issue) needs a custody to issue FROM, or consumables shrinkage hides in the trading rooms.

The shared design rule. Each logical room exists because a DISTINCT QUESTION needs a standing answer: what is rejected and undecided? what is between branches? what is at the subcontractor? what returned and awaits triage? Where the firm genuinely runs the state, the room earns its leaf; where it does not (a single-location firm with no transfers needs no transit room), creating the room manufactures ceremony. The consultant's judgment is the same proportionality every track has practised — model the states the client LIVES, not the states the software offers.

The rooms are custody, not exile. A recurring client misunderstanding, worth pre-empting: stock in quarantine or transit has not left the company — it counts in the firm's stock value, appears in the rollups, and belongs to someone's answerability. The rooms exist to make states VISIBLE, not to make stock disappear; and the monthly read of every logical room's balance and aging (this track's calendar will consolidate it) is how the visible states stay managed instead of sedimenting — because a logical room nobody reads becomes exactly what it was built to prevent: a place where stock quietly stops being anyone's problem.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Stock and money: the custodian's number
lessons.html:
Every warehouse balance is also a naira figure, and this chapter is the bridge this track keeps crossing: stock as VALUE, and the warehouse as a custody of company money that happens to sit on shelves.

How value gets there. Each ledger entry carries valuation: goods arrive at their landed cost (the Procurement 6 truth — PO rate plus allocated charges), leave at the valuation the method computes (module 5 teaches FIFO and moving-average mechanics), and the item-at-warehouse balance is therefore both a quantity AND an amount. Summed per warehouse: the warehouse-wise stock value — Central holding ₦48m, Ibadan ₦11m, Quarantine ₦600k, In-Transit ₦2.1m — and summed altogether, the stock asset the balance sheet reports. The operational reading and the accountant's reading are the same numbers at different rollups, which is exactly why the gate disciplines mattered: a receipt posted wrong is a misstatement, not a typo.

The custodian's number. Attach the value to the accountability and warehouse management changes character: the Ibadan storekeeper is not minding shelves — they are answerable for ₦11m of company assets, and the systems this track teaches (documents for every movement, counts on a cadence, variances investigated) are how that answerability is made fair: the custodian who moves stock only by documents can PROVE their custody; the one who obliges undocumented favours cannot, and inherits every difference as suspicion. Framed this way in training, the disciplines stop being bureaucracy and become the storekeeper's own protection — the framing that makes go-live adoption stick.

Value concentrates attention. The warehouse-wise value read orders the priorities: the counting programme weights toward where the money sits (module 4's cycle design); security and access follow value; and the logical rooms' readings become money readings — ₦600k aging in quarantine is a decision backlog with interest, ₦2.1m in transit is working capital on wheels. The MD who will not read a stock report will read this one, and the consultant should hand it to them monthly.

Shrinkage is the gap's name. Where the ledger says more than the shelf holds, the difference has a value and a family of causes — unrecorded movements, theft, damage never written, gate errors compounding — and module 4 (counting) plus module 7 (the shrinkage trend) turn it from an annual shock into a managed number. For now, hold the accounting shape: the variance a count confirms becomes a written adjustment with a naira cost, landing where the accountant directs — visible, owned, trended. The firm that knows its shrinkage rate manages it; the firm that discovers it annually budgets by superstition.

The bridge's rule. Every operational stock decision is silently a money decision — the transfer is value moving between custodies, the write-off is value leaving with a signature, the count variance is value confessing. This track teaches the operations; the money meaning rides every one of them, and the consultant who narrates BOTH — this movement, this value, this accountability — is teaching inventory the way owners hear it.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Defaults & the choosing of warehouses
lessons.html:
Documents move stock, and every document must answer: WHICH warehouse? The answer should almost never be a human deciding at speed — it should be a default, designed once. This chapter wires the tree to the documents.

The default chain. Warehouse selection resolves top-down: the item's default warehouse (per company — and where the setup supports it, per item-and-branch context) seeds document rows; document-level defaults (the receiving warehouse on a purchase document, the source on a delivery) override per transaction; and the row-level field remains editable for the genuine exception. The design goal from Chapter 2, restated as configuration: every routine flow lands in the right leaf with zero human choices — replenishment receipts into Central, branch sales out of the branch store, rejections into that branch's quarantine — because the human at speed picks the top of the dropdown, and the top of the dropdown is how Ibadan's stock ends up in Abeokuta.

Per-flow defaults, walked. The implementation checklist: purchase receiving defaults to the central store (or the branch, where branches receive directly — a policy decided, not assumed); sales and POS at each branch default to THAT branch's leaf (the per-branch default the multi-location setup lives or dies by); stock entries for issues default from the facilities store; return flows default into staging/quarantine, never silently into sellable. Each default is a sentence of policy — we receive centrally; branches sell their own stock; consumables issue from facilities — and the consultant reads the sentences back to the client before wiring them, because a default nobody chose is still a policy, just an accidental one.

The wrong-warehouse disease. The most routine ticket in multi-location support: stock posted to the wrong leaf — the receipt into the wrong branch, the sale out of a store that never held the goods, the transfer's destination mistyped. The damage is quiet and compounding: two warehouses now both lie (one high, one low), counts at both will surprise, and negative-stock pressure builds where the goods were never booked (module 5 meets what negative stock does to valuation). The response pattern: diagnose from the ledger (Chapter 3's read — the mispost has a document, a date, and an author), correct by MOVEMENT (a transfer putting the stock where it physically is — never an edit, the append-only law), and fix the DEFAULT or permission that made the wrong choice easy — because a mispost is almost never a careless person; it is a dropdown that offered the wrong thing first.

Restriction as the stronger wire. Beyond defaults, the permission layer can BIND: branch users restricted to their branch's warehouses so the wrong leaf is not merely un-defaulted but unavailable. The trade is flexibility for safety, and the multi-branch answer is usually safety — the Ikeja cashier has no honest reason to move Abeokuta's stock, and the restriction that prevents it prevents the ticket, the recount, and the argument. Module 8 owns the full permissions posture; plant the principle here: defaults make the right choice easy; restrictions make the wrong choice impossible; a mature setup uses both.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: designing HealthTrade's network
lessons.html:
HealthTrade — whose suppliers, purchases, and money the Procurement track built — now gets its warehouse constitution. The design session, run as Chapters 1-7 taught it.

Step 1 — the custody list (Ch. 1-2). The walk-through with the MD and the storekeepers lists the real custodies: the Central store (Surulere), two branch stock rooms (Ibadan, Abeokuta), the quarantine bay inside Central, goods moving between locations weekly, consumables (cleaning, stationery) currently living — badly — on a corner of Central's racking, the repacker holding bulk paracetamol (the Procurement 8 subcontract), and returns arriving at whichever counter the customer chose. Eight distinct answerabilities; the shelf-vs-warehouse line holds twice (the fridge inside Central: same custodian, location detail, NOT a warehouse; the consumables corner: different question entirely — its own room).

Step 2 — the tree (Ch. 2, 5). Drawn shallow: All Warehouses → Central Store, Central Quarantine, Facilities Store, In-Transit, Repacker (Subcontract), and a Branches group holding Ibadan Store and Abeokuta Store (each with its small quarantine leaf — the branch that rejects a delivery needs its own bay). Returns staging is FOLDED into quarantine for now — the volume does not yet earn a room, and the decision is written down with its revisit trigger (if return triage exceeds a shelf, split it). Names patterned, branch-first; three levels nowhere exceeded.

Step 3 — the defaults wired (Ch. 7). Purchasing receives to Central (the Procurement 3 policy — branches replenish by transfer, never buy retail); each branch's sales default out of its own store; issues default from Facilities; rejections default to the local quarantine. Branch users are RESTRICTED to their branch leaves plus read on Central (they may see what they can request — module 6's flows will use it). The defaults are read back as policy sentences and the MD signs the page.

Step 4 — the first reads (Ch. 3-6). Week one's numbers, walked with the team: the warehouse-wise value (Central ₦48m, branches ₦9m and ₦7m, quarantine ₦140k, transit ₦800k mid-week, repacker ₦1.2m) — the MD's monthly page from day one, each figure introduced as somebody's custody. A bin read run live for PARA-500 at Ibadan: actual 96, reserved 40 (the weekend's counter orders), incoming 60 (Tuesday's transfer, in transit now), projected 116 — and the storekeeper's but the shelf shows 96 becomes the four-numbers lesson on the spot. One ledger walk: a surprising Abeokuta balance decomposed entry by entry to a receipt posted there in error during setup week — corrected by transfer (the stock is physically at Central), the default that allowed it tightened, the append-only law demonstrated better than any slide.

What the design bought (Ch. 9 previews). Every place stock can be now has a name, a value, and an owner; every routine flow lands right unattended; the logical rooms make rejection, transit, and subcontract states visible instead of anecdotal; and the modules ahead — movements, counting, valuation, the network — inherit a floor that can carry them. The constitution took one afternoon; the alternative is discovering it piecemeal through a year of tickets.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the first law
lessons.html:
The architecture layer's scar tissue — the design mistakes that surface as everyone else's tickets for years. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — warehouse sprawl. Symptom: forty warehouses for an eleven-person firm; nobody can say what half are for. Disease: places created per whim — a warehouse per shelf, per project, per mood (Ch. 2) — custody diluted until no balance is anyone's answer. Fix: the accountability test applied ruthlessly in a consolidation pass — stock moved by documented transfers into the custodies that are real, empty husks disabled; and creation rights narrowed so the tree grows by decision, not convenience.

Pattern 2 — the flat sixty. Symptom: every leaf a direct child of the root; branch reporting assembled by hand each month. Disease: the tree grown without groups (Ch. 2) — structure never designed, only accumulated. Fix: groups introduced and leaves re-parented (structure is re-shapeable; this is the cheap fix in the family) to mirror how the firm actually asks its questions.

Pattern 3 — the room with no twin. Symptom: a physical storeroom whose stock lives, in the books, inside a neighbouring warehouse; differences there are invisible by construction. Disease: custody without a leaf (Ch. 2, 5) — the map missing a territory. Fix: the leaf created, a counted opening moved in by document, defaults corrected — and its mirror twin hunted in the same pass: system warehouses with no physical meaning, absorbing misc postings as a valued junk drawer.

Pattern 4 — actual-only decisions. Symptom: sales promised off the visible shelf while orders held it; purchases panicked while a delivery rode the road. Disease: the four numbers unread (Ch. 4) — decisions made on a quarter of the position. Fix: the bin literacy taught (projected as the deciding number), and the promise hygiene enforced upstream — the ghost and phantom sweeps this track now has standing to demand.

Pattern 5 — the unread logical rooms. Symptom: quarantine holds eleven months of undecided stock; the transit room's balance never returns to zero. Disease: rooms built for visibility, then never read (Ch. 5) — the states visible to no one become states managed by no one. Fix: each room's balance-and-aging on a named calendar rhythm; a room the firm will not commit to reading is a room to fold back until it will.

Pattern 6 — the wrong-warehouse epidemic. Symptom: recurring misposts between branches; counts at both keep surprising. Disease: defaults undesigned and permissions unbound (Ch. 7) — the dropdown offering the wrong leaf first to a user allowed to take it. Fix: the mispost corrected by movement, then the default rewired and the restriction applied — the ticket answered at the layer that generated it.

The first law. Selling's laws began with masters; Procurement's began with the supply base; this track's begins with the map: the warehouse tree is the map of custody — every place stock can be is named, valued, and owned, and stock lives only in named places. Design the map from accountability, wire the defaults so documents walk it unattended, keep the logical rooms read, and the ledger beneath it all stays a book worth believing. Seven modules stand on this floor; module 2 starts moving stock across it.

stock_entries.title: Inventory 2 — Stock Entries & Internal Movements
stock_entries.desc: The internal movement family: the Stock Entry's purposes, the boundary law against trading through it, consumption issues and governed write-offs, honest valuation on receipts, one-step and two-step transfers with the in-transit disciplines, and repacking with yield honesty.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Stock Entry & its purposes
lessons.html:
Module 1 built the map; this module moves stock across it. The instrument is the Stock Entry — the document family for movements that have no commercial counterparty: nothing is being bought or sold; stock is simply appearing, disappearing, or changing rooms inside your own custody. One doctype, several purposes, and the purpose — exactly as it was on the Material Request — decides the machinery.

  • Material Receipt — stock IN with no supplier transaction behind it: the genuine appearance (found stock surfacing at a count's edge, promotional goods arriving free, and — carefully policed — certain opening flows). Because value enters with quantity, the receipt DEMANDS a valuation rate: Chapter 4 owns the discipline.
  • Material Issue — stock OUT with no customer: internal consumption (the cleaning supplies, the spare parts), and value leaving deliberately (the write-off of expired or damaged goods). The out-going value lands somewhere in the books, which makes every issue an expense event wearing warehouse clothes: Chapter 3.
  • Material Transfer — stock BETWEEN two of your own leaves: same total, different rooms, custody handed over. One-step for the trivial case (Chapter 5), two-step through the transit room for real distance (Chapter 6).
  • Repack — stock TRANSFORMED: consume these items, produce those, value flowing from inputs to outputs — the bulk carton becoming retail strips without a subcontractor (Chapter 7).

The shared anatomy. Whatever the purpose: a posting date and time (the chronology law from module 1 — this document writes the ledger, so its date is testimony); rows of item, quantity, UOM with its conversion (the arithmetic never rests); source warehouse, target warehouse, or both, per the purpose's shape; and the reason — the remark or reference that answers, years later, WHY this movement happened. A trading document's why is its counterparty and its chain; a stock entry's why is a sentence a human wrote, which is precisely why Chapter 2's boundary matters and why an unexplained stock entry is this track's version of an unsigned cheque.

Submission's weight. A submitted stock entry writes the ledger — ins, outs, valuation effects — with everything module 1 taught about that act: irreversible in the ordinary course, correctable only by appended counter-movements, and evidence forever. Draft, check the purpose, the rooms, the quantities, the rate where one is demanded, and the reason; then submit. The whole module is the elaboration of that checklist.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The boundary law: what stock entries are NOT for
lessons.html:
Before the legitimate uses, the conviction that protects them — because the Stock Entry is the most abusable document in the system, and the abuse is always the same one.

The law: trading movements never travel by stock entry. Goods bought arrive by Purchase Receipt against a Purchase Order; goods sold leave by Delivery Note against a Sales Order; returns travel by their return documents. The Stock Entry is for movements with no counterparty — and the moment there is a supplier or a customer on the other side of the goods, using a stock entry amputates everything both trading tracks built:

  • Receive a purchase as Material Receipt and: no PO fulfilment counts down, the three-way match loses its possession leg (the invoice will match nothing — Procurement 7's control disarmed at birth), the supplier's delivery performance vanishes from the record, landed cost has no receipt to attach to, and the valuation rate is whatever a human typed instead of the committed rate travelling. One shortcut, five amputations.
  • Ship a sale as Material Issue and: no order fulfilment moves, no invoice chain exists, the customer's ledger never learns, serial and batch outbound custody breaks, and the revenue the goods represent has left the building as an EXPENSE. This is not a workaround; it is the shape unrecorded sales take.

Why the abuse happens — and the honest answers. The stock entry is FAST: no master needed, no chain, no match — which is exactly the problem, and exactly why it tempts at the busy moments. The situations that drive it, each with its lawful answer: the supplier isn't set up yet — set them up (Procurement 1's gate exists for this, and the emergency onboarding is an hour, not a week); we just need the stock in the system NOW — the emergency PO-and-receipt is minutes, and it keeps the chain (Procurement 6's unordered-truck doctrine: even urgency gets a document); it's a tiny cash purchase — the policy's exempted tail exists, written, and even the tail buys through a minimal purchase flow, not a warehouse side door.

The consultant's detection kit. The abuse announces itself in the ledger: Material Receipts with valuation rates suspiciously like supplier prices, Material Issues tracking suspiciously with sales patterns, stock entries clustering at month-end or at one user. The standing audit — stock entries reviewed monthly by purpose, value, and author (Chapter 9 makes it a calendar item) — is cheap; the archaeology after a year of side-door trading is not: unmatched invoices, unmeasurable suppliers, valuation built on typed guesses, and a stock asset the auditor rightly distrusts.

The law's positive face. Held properly, the boundary makes BOTH families trustworthy: every trading movement carries its chain (matchable, measurable, valued by its documents), and every stock entry means what it says — a genuinely internal event, explained by its reason. A ledger where the two never blur is a ledger where every line's ancestry is knowable from its document type alone — which is the property every diagnosis in this track leans on.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Material Issue: consumption & the write-off
lessons.html:
Stock leaves without a customer for two honest reasons — it was USED, or it must be DESTROYED — and the Material Issue serves both, with different governance for each.

Consumption — the routine issue. The cleaning supplies to the floor, the stationery to admin, the spare part to the generator: stock consumed by the firm's own operation. The mechanics: issue FROM the custody that holds it (the Facilities store module 1 gave a room to), quantities in honest UOMs, and the value landing in the right expense context — because an issue is stock value becoming expense, and WHERE it lands (the expense attribution the accountant configures) is what makes consumption visible by department and category instead of dissolving into one anonymous bucket. The operating rhythm: issues recorded AT consumption (the weekly batch that fictionalises Tuesday's usage into Friday's entry is the posting-date disease again), and the consumables reorder loop closing through the same planning fields as everything else — the Facilities store has bins too.

The write-off — value leaving with a signature. Expired stock after the disposal decision, damage beyond negotiation, the quarantine lot whose fate (Procurement 6's fork) resolved to destruction: the Material Issue writes it out of stock and into the write-off's expense home. The governance is proportional to the fact that this is company value being destroyed on someone's say-so: a reason on the document always (the expiry batch numbers, the damage description, the reference to the quarantine decision); an approval line by value (the storekeeper alone does not write off ₦2m — thresholds, like every gate number in these tracks, written); physical destruction actually performed and, for regulated goods, performed per the compliance requirements (pharma disposal has rules, and the write-off document is part of that evidence file, not a substitute for it); and the identity trail closed — expired BATCHES written off by lot, so the batch's biography ends with a documented death, not a disappearance.

The issue is not a dustbin. The disease this chapter must pre-empt: the Material Issue as the place unexplained differences go to die — the count that came up short quietly issued out as consumption, shrinkage laundered into expense lines a little every week. The tells: issue volumes trending with no operational story, issues without references, one author issuing everything. The law: differences are for the reconciliation (module 4) — counted, investigated, adjusted in the open with their own document and their own trend line; consumption is for things actually consumed. Blur them and the firm loses its shrinkage number, which means losing the ability to manage the very leak being hidden.

Reading issues as management. Done honestly, the issue history is a report the owner wants: consumables cost by month and department, write-off value by reason (expiry vs damage — the first indicts buying quantities, the second indicts handling), and the trend that says whether the generator eats more spares this year than last. The document that records value leaving is also the document that explains it — the whole track's philosophy at one desk.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Material Receipt: stock from nowhere, valued honestly
lessons.html:
Stock appearing without a supplier is rare, legitimate, and dangerous in exact proportion to how casually it is valued. This chapter is the short list of honest uses and the one discipline they share.

The honest list. Found stock: the count's edge case — goods physically present that the ledger never knew (the pallet behind the racking, the un-receipted sample that got shelved). Where reconciliation (module 4) is running, found stock usually enters THERE, inside the count's own document; the Material Receipt serves the between-counts discovery that cannot wait. Genuine free goods: promotional stock from a manufacturer with no invoice ever coming — real appearance, no counterparty payable. Opening flows, carefully: go-live stock loading is module 4's set-piece (the reconciliation is the proper instrument, and the Topmost-style disaster — opening stock keyed at selling prices — is convicted there in full); the Material Receipt appears in opening work only for narrow, deliberate cases, and never as the bulk loader.

The discipline: valuation is mandatory and honest. Stock in means value in — the ledger will not take quantity without cost, so the Material Receipt demands a valuation rate per row. The rate is a statement the books will carry forever, so it is derived, not invented: found stock enters at what it would have cost (the item's current valuation or last honest purchase rate — the found pallet of PARA-500 enters at PARA-500's cost, not at zero and not at retail); free goods enter at the value policy the accountant sets (a zero-cost entry is defensible and distorts margin the day the goods sell at full price; a fair-cost entry with the offset the accountant directs is often truer — the point is that this is an ACCOUNTING choice made once, not a warehouse improvisation made per pallet); and every receipt carries its reason and reference, because stock-from-nowhere without a story is exactly what an auditor is trained to circle.

The valuation ripple, previewed. Module 5 teaches the mechanics; plant the intuition now: the entering rate joins the item's valuation stream — under moving average it blends into every subsequent issue's cost; under FIFO it queues at its place. A careless rate on a large receipt therefore poisons COGS for weeks after: the zero-valued found pallet makes the next month's margins look brilliant and mean nothing. The bigger the quantity, the more the rate deserves a second pair of eyes — value thresholds on Material Receipts route to approval exactly as write-offs do, and for the same reason read in reverse: this is company value being CREATED on someone's say-so.

Frequency is the health check. Material Receipts should be RARE. A firm whose ledger shows them weekly has one of three problems: trading through the side door (Chapter 2's abuse — check the rates and patterns), a broken receiving gate upstream (purchases failing into workarounds — fix the gate, not the symptom), or counts so infrequent that found-stock discoveries pile up between them (module 4's cadence answer). The document's proper life is boring: a handful of well-explained appearances a year, each with a rate someone could defend and a story someone recorded.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Material Transfer: the one-step move
lessons.html:
The simplest movement: stock changes rooms, custody changes hands, nothing else changes. The one-step Material Transfer serves the case where the move is effectively INSTANT — and knowing where that case ends is the chapter's real lesson.

The mechanics. Rows carry item, quantity, source warehouse and target warehouse; submission writes both sides at once — OUT of the source, IN to the target, the same moment, the same document. Value travels with the goods at the source's valuation (a transfer never revalues — the goods cost what they cost regardless of the room; module 5 formalises it), identities travel by name (the serials and batches move as themselves, their biographies gaining a line), and the two bins update together: no gap, no limbo, conservation of stock in one document.

Where one-step is right. The moves with no meaningful in-between: within one site (Central floor to Central quarantine after a damage discovery; the fork's manual edition), between adjacent custodies with instant handover (the back store to the sales floor where both are modelled), and any move where dispatch and receipt are the SAME physical act by people standing in the same place. The test: is there a moment when the goods are with neither custodian? No — one-step. Yes — Chapter 6, because that moment needs a room.

The custody handshake. Even instant transfers move accountability, and the small disciplines keep the handshake real: the receiving side acknowledges (in a same-site move this is trivially the same team, but between custodians — floor to warehouse, store to store-within-store — the transfer done TO someone who did not know is how differences get born arguing); quantities counted at handover where the custodians differ (thirty seconds now versus a variance dispute at the next count); and the reason field carrying the why for anything non-routine (the damage transfer to quarantine references what happened — the quarantine review will want it).

What one-step must not stretch to cover. The classic misuse: the Lagos-to-Ibadan transfer entered as one-step because it is fewer clicks. The document happily complies — OUT of Central, IN to Ibadan, the same second — and the ledger now says Ibadan holds stock that is, in the world, on a truck in Ogun State for the next six hours. Every read of Ibadan's bin is wrong until the truck arrives; a count at Ibadan during the window would surprise; and if the truck never arrives, the loss is discovered as an Ibadan shortage — the wrong custody blamed, the investigation starting a room away from the truth. Distance means a custody gap; the custody gap means the transit room; the transit room means the two-step — which is the next chapter, and the reason module 1 built the room before this module needed it.

Volume hygiene. Transfers are the highest-frequency stock entries in a branch network, so their smallest frictions compound: templated rows for the routine weekly moves, defaults per flow (module 1's wiring), and the discipline that transfers are entered by the people MAKING them at the time of making — the pile of transfer paperwork keyed by one clerk on Friday is the posting-date disease at network scale.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The two-step transfer & the in-transit room
lessons.html:
Real distance separates dispatch from receipt, and the two-step transfer is how the system tells the truth about the in-between. This is the mechanical heart of the branch network (module 6 builds the governance; here is the machinery).

The two documents. Step one — dispatch: Central sends 40 cartons to Ibadan; the transfer moves the goods OUT of Central Store and IN to the In-Transit room (module 1's warehouse with no walls). Central's custody has honestly ended; Ibadan's has honestly not begun; the transit room answers for the truck. Step two — receipt: the goods arrive; Ibadan's receiving transfer moves them OUT of In-Transit and IN to Ibadan Store — at the quantities Ibadan actually counts. The receiving side counts exactly as Procurement 6's gate taught, because an inter-branch arrival is a receiving event in every way that matters: count before accepting custody, against the dispatch document, discrepancies recorded as they are.

Why the room changes everything. At every moment, one custody answers: before dispatch, Central; on the road, In-Transit; after receipt, Ibadan. The one-step's lie (Chapter 5) is structurally impossible — no bin ever claims goods it does not hold. And the failure cases become VISIBLE instead of misattributed: the truck that arrives short leaves the shortfall IN the transit room — a named, valued, investigable difference between what left and what arrived, sitting in the exact custody where the loss occurred — rather than surfacing weeks later as an Ibadan count variance blamed on the wrong storekeeper. Transit shrinkage is real in Nigerian logistics; the two-step is what makes it a managed number with a location instead of an argument between branches.

The transit disciplines. Three, all cheap: reference discipline — dispatch and receipt documents linked (the receipt made against the dispatch, remainder logic pre-filling exactly as every create-from in these tracks), the truck's waybill referenced, so the road has a paper trail; the aging read — the transit room's balance, aged: anything older than the longest honest journey is an incident (truck delayed, receipt never entered, or goods gone), worked from a standing list — module 1 planted this diagnostic, and here is its operation: the transit room returns to zero between runs in a healthy network, and its aging report is the earliest smoke detector the network has; the shortfall protocol — arrival differences investigated from the transit balance while the trail is hot (the driver, the waybill, the seals), resolved by the honest instrument: recovered goods received, confirmed losses written off FROM transit with the write-off's governance (Chapter 3 — value leaving with a signature), never quietly absorbed by receiving inflated quantities to make the room zero out.

Receiving discipline at the branch. The arriving branch signs for custody, so the gate rules apply in miniature: count against the dispatch note, not the driver's word; accept what arrived, record what did not; identities confirmed (the batches that left are the batches that arrived — the swap en route is a real fraud pattern, and batch-level receiving is what catches it). A branch that receives casually inherits every road-side difference as its own unexplained variance — the framing (module 1's custodian's number) that makes branch teams WANT the discipline.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Repack: transformation without a factory
lessons.html:
Between moving stock and manufacturing it sits a common trading need: the SAME goods in a DIFFERENT form — the bulk carton become retail strips, the 25kg sack become 1kg packs, the assorted lot broken into singles. The Repack purpose serves it, and its craft is mostly about value and honesty.

The mechanics. One stock entry, two kinds of row: consumed rows (the inputs, OUT of their warehouse — one bulk carton of 100 strips) and produced rows (the outputs, IN — 100 retail strip units, plus, where honest, the packaging materials consumed alongside). Value flows conserved: the outputs enter at the inputs' total value (allocated across produced rows — by the sensible basis where multiple outputs), so no value is created or destroyed by changing the box. Quantity changes; UOM changes; identity persists where tracked — the produced strips carry the source batch and its expiry, because repacking a batch does not launder its provenance (the NAFDAC chain survives the scissors, and the entry's mapping is what proves it).

The yield honesty. Real repacking has losses — the torn strip, the spillage from the sack — and the honest entry records the yield as it happened: 100 in, 98 saleable out, 2 to the damage row (written off with Chapter 3's governance, or quarantined per policy). The dishonest patterns to refuse: producing 100 from 98's worth of reality (the shortfall surfacing at the next count, blamed on custody), and the standing yield loss never trended (repack loss is a rate to WATCH — a packing team whose 2% becomes 5% is a conversation the trend triggers, exactly the subcontractor yield logic of Procurement 8 brought in-house).

Where repack ends and other machinery begins. The boundary judgment, three ways: repack vs subcontract — the transformation done by an OUTSIDE party with your materials is Procurement 8's subcontract flow (service purchased, supplier-side custody), not a repack entry pretending the repacker doesn't exist; repack vs manufacturing — combining DIFFERENT materials into a genuinely new product (formulation, assembly with recipes, work-in-progress stages) is the manufacturing module's terrain, with its own masters and costing — the repack entry stretched over real manufacturing produces costs nobody can defend; repack vs UOM — and the subtlest: if the carton and the strip are the SAME item in different UOMs with a clean conversion, much selling and stocking needs no repack at all (Buying 2's UOM architecture already lets one item live in both units) — the repack exists for where the retail form is a DIFFERENT item (own code, own barcode, own price list line), which is an item-architecture decision made deliberately at setup, not per entry. The consultant who can walk a client through those three boundaries in ten minutes has saved them either a missing module or a pile of needless entries.

Governance, briefly. Repack entries create sellable retail stock from bulk, so the same value-threshold eyes apply: reasons and references routine, the yield trend on the monthly read, and the mapping of batches through the transformation spot-checked — because the entry that says which batch became which strips is, for regulated goods, a compliance document wearing warehouse clothes.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: a month of movements at HealthTrade
lessons.html:
The network module 1 designed now runs a month of internal movements. Every chapter clocks in; every movement names its document.

Week 1 — the routine floor (Ch. 3). Facilities issues run at consumption: cleaning supplies Tuesday, stationery Thursday, each landing in its expense attribution — the month-end consumables read will show admin ₦38k, floor ₦52k, and the MD will see consumption by department for the first time. One write-off: a water-damaged carton discovered shelf-side, transferred one-step to Central Quarantine (Ch. 5 — same site, instant custody), then written off after the weekly quarantine review with photos referenced and the ₦86k landing in damage expense under the storekeeper-plus-manager threshold rule.

Week 2 — the network breathes (Ch. 6). The weekly Ibadan run: dispatch transfer moves 40 cartons PARA-500 plus twelve lines OUT of Central, IN to In-Transit, waybill referenced. Ibadan receives next morning AGAINST the dispatch: thirteen lines count clean; one line — cough syrup — counts 18 of 20. The receipt takes 18; the shortfall of 2 stays IN transit, visible, valued (₦21k), investigated same-day while the trail is hot: the waybill shows 20 loaded, the driver's second drop-point had no syrup on its manifest, the seals were intact at Ibadan... and the recount at Central finds 2 bottles mis-picked into the NEXT run's staging. Recovered: received into Ibadan on the following run's documents, transit back to zero. Total cost: one hour. The counterfactual — a one-step transfer — would have discovered nothing until Ibadan's next count surprised, and blamed the wrong branch.

Week 3 — the repack (Ch. 7). The retail chain's blister-strip demand outgrows the subcontractor's monthly run, and small top-ups move in-house: a repack entry consumes 2 bulk cartons (200 strips' worth) plus packaging sleeves, produces 196 retail strip units carrying batch B-1152 and its expiry, and writes 4 damaged strips to the loss row — a 2% yield, logged, joining the trend the subcontractor's own 3% already lives on. The retail item is a DIFFERENT item by deliberate setup (own barcode, own price line) — the boundary conversation was had at design, which is why the entry is routine instead of an argument.

Week 4 — the appearance and the audit (Ch. 2, 4). A shelf reorganisation surfaces a pallet of 6 cartons of vitamin syrup the ledger never knew — un-receipted during a chaotic delivery month before go-live. The Material Receipt enters it with a story: reason recorded, valued at the item's current valuation rate (₦4,200/carton — derived from the last honest purchase, not guessed), and flagged to the accountant for the offset. Month-end, the standing stock-entry audit runs: entries by purpose, value, and author — one page, five minutes, nothing anomalous: Material Receipts rare (one, explained), issues tracking operations, transfers clearing transit, the repack yield on trend. The boring page IS the control working.

The month's ledger read (Ch. 1-9). Every internal movement carries a purpose, a room, a reason; the transit room slept at zero six nights in seven; value left only with signatures; and the one appearance had a story and a defensible rate. Module 4 will now test this ledger against the shelves — and because this month was disciplined, the count will be a confirmation, not a confession.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the second law
lessons.html:
The movement layer's scar tissue. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — trading through the side door. Symptom: Material Receipts at supplier-like rates; issues tracking sales. Disease: the boundary law broken (Ch. 2) — the match disarmed, suppliers unmeasurable, valuation typed, revenue leaving as expense. Fix: the lawful flows restored with their emergency speeds (the fast PO exists precisely so the side door has no excuse), the monthly stock-entry audit standing, and the historical mess reconciled deliberately with the accountant.

Pattern 2 — the issue as dustbin. Symptom: consumption climbing with no operational story; count variances mysteriously scarce. Disease: shrinkage laundered through issues (Ch. 3) — differences buried where the reconciliation should have surfaced them, the shrinkage number destroyed. Fix: differences routed to module 4's instrument exclusively; issue references required; the issues-by-author-and-trend read that makes the laundering visible.

Pattern 3 — the unvalued appearance. Symptom: found stock entered at zero (or at retail); margins swinging weirdly after. Disease: valuation improvised at the Material Receipt (Ch. 4) — the careless rate poisoning the costing stream for weeks. Fix: rates derived from the item's honest cost, the accountant's offset policy applied, value thresholds routing large receipts to approval — created value gets the same eyes as destroyed value.

Pattern 4 — distance one-stepped. Symptom: branch bins right eventually, wrong for hours or days; road losses surfacing as branch count variances; inter-branch blame. Disease: the one-step stretched over a custody gap (Ch. 5) — the ledger asserting arrivals that have not happened. Fix: the two-step with the transit room for anything with a road in it; the one-step reserved for moves where dispatch and receipt are one act.

Pattern 5 — the transit room that never empties. Symptom: a standing in-transit balance nobody can itemise. Disease: receipts never entered, shortfalls never resolved, the room unread (Ch. 6) — the network's smoke detector unplugged. Fix: the aging read on the weekly rhythm, receipt-against-dispatch as unskippable routine, shortfalls investigated hot and resolved by the honest instruments — received, or written off from transit with governance.

Pattern 6 — yields imagined. Symptom: repacks always produce perfectly; counts after repacking surprise. Disease: yield dishonesty (Ch. 7) — losses unrecorded at the entry, surfacing later as custody variances. Fix: the loss row as routine, the yield trend watched, and the boundary check that the operation belongs in repack at all.

The second law. Module 1: the warehouse tree is the map of custody. This module adds: stock moves only by documents, and every movement names its purpose — where a trading counterparty exists, the trading chain carries the goods; where none does, the reason is the counterparty. Receipts demand honest value, issues demand honest destinations, transfers demand honest custody at every moment of the journey, and transformations demand honest yields. A ledger whose movements all obey this law can be read like a diary; module 4 is about checking that diary against the world — the count — and a firm that kept this module's disciplines walks into that count unafraid.
