serial_batch.title: Inventory 3 — Serial & Batch Operations
serial_batch.desc: The identity layer in full: the two identity systems and the architecture decision, serial and batch lifecycles, expiry operations with FEFO and the markdown ladder, the recall run-book, identity hygiene and audits, and identity in the daily flow.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Two identity systems, one architecture decision
lessons.html:
Both trading tracks met identity at their gates — Selling reading it out, Procurement writing it in. This module is identity's own curriculum: the warehouse lives with these records every day, and the warehouse is where they earn their keep or rot.

The two systems, distinguished precisely. A serial number makes each UNIT an individual: one serial, one physical thing, one biography — received here, sits there, delivered to them, returned, serviced. A serial exists in exactly one place at a time (or one state: delivered, in stock, returned), which is what makes it a biography rather than a tally. A batch makes units MEMBERS of a lot: one batch, many units, one shared story — the same production run, the same expiry, the same recall fate. A batch, unlike a serial, lives in many places at once: B-1147 can hold 60 cartons at Central, 25 at Ibadan, 5 in transit, and the batch's position is a per-warehouse read. Serial answers which one?; batch answers which lot, and how much of it, where?

What each enables — the coverage bought. Serials buy: warranty and service anchoring (the chiller's plate number opening its file), theft and swap detection (the unit that returns is provably the unit that left), unit-level custody in transfers and audits. Batches buy: expiry management and FEFO (Chapter 4), the recall in both directions (Chapter 5), and quality attribution by production run. Neither is free: every gate slows by the capture minutes, every movement carries the bookkeeping, and the flags are why — which makes the flag decision an ARCHITECTURE decision, not a preference.

The flag decision, revisited as architecture. Buying 2 set the flags at item creation; this chapter is the reasoning at full depth. Serialize where the unit is individually valuable, serviceable, or fraud-attractive (equipment, devices, high-value electronics); batch where goods expire, are regulated, or fail by production run (pharma, food, cosmetics — for your clients, most of the shelf); NEITHER where the item is cheap, stable, and interchangeable (the biro needs no biography). The costs of getting it wrong are asymmetric and both real: flags ON without operational need is a permanent tax on every gate for coverage nobody reads (Chapter 9's identity theatre); flags OFF where regulation or service needs them is a retrofit — and the retrofit is genuinely painful: existing unidentified stock cannot retroactively acquire provenance, so the transition is a managed cutover (existing stock counted into identified form with honest unknowns marked), not a checkbox. Decide at item birth with the ten-year view; the item architecture chapter said it, and now you can see everything it was protecting.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The serial lifecycle: a biography in states
lessons.html:
A serialized unit's record is a small dossier the system maintains for life. Reading and trusting that dossier is the skill; this chapter walks the life.

Birth. The serial is born on a Purchase Receipt (Procurement 6's most consequential data entry): captured from the physical unit — the plate, the engraving, the manufacturer's label — never from the packing list. From that entry the dossier opens: item, supplier, purchase document, receipt date, cost. Everything after appends.

The states of a life. At any moment the serial is in exactly one state, and the state answers the operational question: in stock — at a named warehouse (the serial's location is a fact, not a search); in transit — riding a two-step transfer, the room answering for it by name; delivered — with a named customer via a named Delivery Note (the warranty clock's anchor, the proof in any dispute about what was supplied when); returned — back through the return documents, the biography recording the round trip and the triage verdict (restock, quarantine, repair path); and terminal states — written off with its governance, or expired from the system's concern by policy. The dossier is the union of the states: any serial, any moment, one screen answers where it is, where it has been, and by which documents.

Movements by name. Serialized stock never moves as a quantity — every movement names its serials: the transfer lists which units ride the truck (and the receiving branch confirms those units arrived — the swap-en-route catch), the delivery lists which units the customer got (the exact-unit dispute-ender), the write-off names its dead. The bookkeeping cost is real and the purchase is precision: quantity-level custody says three chillers left; serial-level custody says WHICH three, and only one of those statements survives contact with a warranty claim, a theft investigation, or an insurance file.

The service anchor. For equipment trade, the serial is where after-sales lives: the service history appended per unit, the warranty window computed from the delivery's date, the repeat-failure pattern visible per unit and per batch-of-units (three failures on units from one receipt is a supplier conversation with evidence). The consultant selling serialization to a client sells THIS — not compliance, but the end of every argument that begins the one we bought from you: the dossier either shows that unit, that date, that document — or shows the unit was never yours, which ends a different and more expensive argument (the counterfeit warranty claim, the unit bought elsewhere seeking your service). The impossible return from Selling 5 is this chapter's machinery doing its outbound job.

Reading the dossier as diagnosis. Like the stock ledger it lives inside, the serial's history is the first stop when a unit's story is disputed: the state that surprises decomposes into its documents. A serial in stock that cannot be found is a count matter (module 4); a serial delivered that the customer denies is a POD matter (the DN's evidence); a serial that appears twice is Chapter 6's ghost hunt. The dossier does not argue; it cites.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The batch lifecycle: the lot across the network
lessons.html:
A batch is a population, and managing it is demography: how much of lot B-1147 exists, where, in what states, expiring when. The mechanics differ from serials in exactly the ways that matter operationally.

Birth and the shared facts. The batch is born at receipt — lot number and expiry keyed from the physical cartons (the entry FEFO and the recall both stand on). Its shared facts bind every member unit: one expiry, one supplier provenance (via the receipt), one quality fate. Multiple receipts can feed one batch (the same lot arriving in two drops — the same lot number keys to the same batch record) and one item holds many live batches simultaneously — the normal state of a pharmacy shelf.

The per-warehouse position. Unlike a serial, a batch disperses: its balance is a GRID — batch × warehouse — and the batch-wise stock read answers the demographic questions: B-1147 holds 60 at Central, 25 at Ibadan, 5 in transit; B-1152, younger, holds 180 at Central untouched. Movements draw down the batch at the source and build it at the target — the batch splits across rooms without losing identity, and every split is ledgered. The read matters daily (which batch does Ibadan actually hold?) and existentially in the recall (Chapter 5's first question is exactly this grid).

Batches do not merge. The rule with no exceptions: two lots are two lots forever. The temptation arrives at the shelf (the half-carton of B-1147 topped up from B-1152's carton — one bin, mixed physically) and at the desk (the clerk recording the mixed shelf as one batch for tidiness). Physical mixing may be a shelf reality the firm manages (or prohibits — pharma practice generally prohibits it precisely for this reason); LEDGER mixing is never acceptable: the recorded quantities stay per-batch, picked per-batch, sold per-batch — because a merged record cannot be unmerged the day NAFDAC names one of the two lots, and the merged shelf's whole quantity inherits the recall. Keep lots distinct in the record, and where the physical shelf must hold two, the pick discipline (Chapter 4's FEFO plus batch selection at the till) keeps the record true.

Batch attributes beyond expiry. The batch record carries what the lot shares: manufacturing date where captured, the supplier's own lot references (the cross-walk NAFDAC correspondence uses), and quality notes appended by inspections or incidents — the batch that drew a customer complaint carries the note, and the second complaint against the same lot is a pattern the record surfaces (quarantine the remainder pending review: the fork, batch-triggered).

The batch as cost carrier. Where valuation runs at batch granularity, each lot carries its own cost story (the January import's landed rate vs March's), and margin reads per batch become possible — the operational payoff being honest answers to are we making money on the old stock we discounted? Module 5 owns valuation's mechanics; plant the connection: identity granularity and cost granularity are the same decision seen from two chairs.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Expiry operations: the horizon, FEFO & the markdown
lessons.html:
For your pharmacy, food, and FMCG clients, expiry is the identity system's daily workout — and the difference between a managed horizon and an annual write-off shock is entirely operational discipline. This chapter is that discipline.

The horizon read. The standing report: batch balances by days-to-expiry — expired (should be zero in stock, quarantined pending disposal), 0-30 days, 31-60, 61-90, beyond. Read weekly at minimum, per warehouse (the network's expiry is not one number: Central's fresh pallets and Ibadan's aging shelf are different problems), and read as a WORKLIST: each near bucket's lines carry a decision owner. The horizon's whole purpose is converting expiry from an event that happens TO the firm into a pipeline the firm works.

FEFO in operation. First-Expired-First-Out: picks and sales draw the earliest-expiring batch first. The system's role is suggestion and enforcement at the pick/sale moment (the batch offered first is the earliest-dated with stock at that warehouse); the human role is compliance and honest exception — the override exists (the customer who needs the longest dating for their own shelf life gets it; an export order's minimum-dating clause binds), and the override is LOGGED, because habitual override is how FEFO dies quietly: the pickers grabbing the front row, the fresh batch bleeding out while the old one ages to death at the back. The FEFO-compliance read (overrides by user and reason, monthly) is the discipline's heartbeat — near-total compliance with occasional explained exceptions is health; drift is the write-off line's future.

The markdown ladder. Between fresh and dead sits the decision zone, and the firm's SHORT-DATING POLICY is a ladder written in advance: at N days remaining, flag for push (front-of-shelf, staff awareness); at M days, markdown per the discount authority (Selling 3's rules — the policy IS a pricing rule, pre-approved, not a per-carton negotiation); at the floor, the channels of last honest resort where the trade allows (the bulk-to-institutional sale with dating disclosed); past saleable, quarantine for disposal. Every rung is cheaper than the rung below it, which is the whole argument for working the horizon early: the ₦9,600 carton sold at ₦8,200 in month one of the window beats the ₦9,600 write-off in month three, every time, and the ladder makes the arithmetic routine instead of painful.

The disposal endgame. Expired regulated goods exit through governance, not the bin: quarantined on expiry (out of sellable truth the day the date passes — the horizon read's expired bucket must be empty of SELLABLE stock, always), written off with Inv 2's signatures and batch-level identity, and physically destroyed per the compliance regime — pharma disposal is witnessed, documented, and filed, with the write-off document part of the evidence chain, not a substitute for it. The batch biography ends: born at receipt, lived across the grid, died with paperwork.

The upstream feedback. Expiry losses are a message, and the horizon's trend is the envelope: chronic short-dating losses on a line indict buying quantities (Procurement 2-3's planning fields — buying past the sell-through), gate acceptance (Procurement 6's minimum-dating rule too loose), or velocity assumptions (the item slowed and the buying never heard). The monthly expiry-loss read, by item and cause, is the warehouse telling procurement the truth — and this track giving the earlier tracks their feedback loop.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The recall run-book
lessons.html:
The recall is the identity system's final exam, and it is taken under time pressure with a regulator watching. This chapter turns the drill both earlier tracks previewed into a RUN-BOOK — the written procedure a competent team executes in hours, not weeks.

The trigger. NAFDAC (or the manufacturer) names a batch. The clock starts. The run-book's steps, in order, each with its instrument:

  • Step 1 — freeze the batch (minutes). The named lot is blocked from sale and movement network-wide: batch-level hold, tills and pickers warned, the batch's per-warehouse grid (Chapter 3) pulled as the working document. Nothing else proceeds until nothing of the lot can move.
  • Step 2 — the inbound trace (minutes). The receipt(s) that brought the batch: supplier, PO, dates, quantities, the supplier's own lot references and documentation from the shipment file (Procurement 1 and 6 built this shelf; today it is opened). This is the packet the NAFDAC and manufacturer correspondence runs on.
  • Step 3 — the holdings sweep (within the hour). Current stock of the lot, per warehouse INCLUDING the logical rooms — the transit balance, the quarantine bay, the repacker's supplier-side room (the repack mapping from Inv 2 traces which produced strips carry the lot). Physical verification against the grid: the counted lot moved to quarantine, every warehouse confirming.
  • Step 4 — the outbound trace (within hours). Every Delivery Note and sale carrying the batch: customers, branches, quantities, dates — Selling 5's drill executed from the warehouse chair. The output is the CONTACT LIST: who must be told, what they received, when.
  • Step 5 — customer contact & retrieval. Per the firm's recall policy and the regulator's instruction: notifications out (documented), returns in through the return machinery with batch identity confirmed at the gate (what comes back is provably the lot), retrieved stock into quarantine joining the sweep.
  • Step 6 — the reconciliation. The closing arithmetic, and the step that separates a defensible recall from a hopeful one: received − sold − held − returned − written-off = zero, per warehouse, documented. Every unit of the lot accounted for by a ledger line; the residual, if any, named and hunted. This page is what the regulator, the manufacturer, and your own counsel each want, and the identity disciplines of two tracks exist so this page can be produced.

The run-book as artifact. Written, owned, and DRILLED: the annual mock recall (pick a batch, run the book, time it) is cheap insurance that finds the gaps on a Tuesday instead of during the real letter — the transit room someone forgot to sweep, the branch that receives batch-blind, the repack mapping nobody spot-checked. Target times are set honestly per the firm (hours for a disciplined single-region network) and the mock's timing is the identity system's health certificate. A firm that can produce the reconciliation page in four hours is a firm whose gates, movements, and records all held; every failure mode in this module's Chapter 9 shows up first as a mock-recall gap.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Identity hygiene: ghosts, orphans & the audits
lessons.html:
Identity records drift from reality exactly as quantities do, and the drift has its own bestiary. This chapter names the creatures and installs the audits that hunt them.

The bestiary. Ghost serials: recorded units that do not physically exist — born from packing-list capture (the list said five, four arrived), duplicate keying, or receipts of units later swapped. A ghost sits in stock forever, inflates the count expectation, and surfaces as the impossible situation (the unit sold that was never here, the audit that cannot find it). Orphan batches: quantity in a batch the physical shelf cannot show, or shelf stock whose batch the record cannot name — born from batch-blind movements (the transfer that carried quantity but not lot), lazy till picks (sold from B-1147 on screen, handed from B-1152 by hand), and capture skipped at busy gates. Orphans are the recall's nightmare: the reconciliation that will not zero. The double life: one physical unit under two records (re-keyed on a correction that never voided the original) — the audit finds it as a serial in two states at once.

The serial audit. Periodic, warehouse by warehouse: the system's in-stock serial list against a physical scan or sight of the units. Three outcomes per line: matched (the healthy majority), recorded-not-found (ghost candidates — investigated before written off: mis-shelved? in an unrecorded state? actually gone, which is a custody matter for module 4's machinery), found-not-recorded (the reverse ghost — a unit with no record, entered with Inv 2's found-stock discipline and a hard look at which gate leaked). Cadence follows value: high-value serial stock quarterly; the audit rides the counting programme module 4 builds rather than duplicating it.

The batch integrity read. The batch equivalent, run as arithmetic before it is run as legwork: per item, the sum of batch balances must equal the bin's actual (a gap means quantity moving batch-blind somewhere — find the leaking document type); expired batches must show zero sellable (the horizon's standing rule); and the spot-check at counts — shelf cartons' printed lots against the recorded batch mix for that warehouse — catches the till-pick drift (screen says B-1147, hand said B-1152) before it compounds. Where drift is found, the correction is a documented batch adjustment with a reason, and the FIX is upstream: the till discipline retrained, the gate's capture tightened, the transfer receiving made batch-level (Inv 2's rule, now with its enforcement audit).

Overrides and exceptions, read monthly. The identity system's pressure valves — FEFO overrides, manual batch selections, serial substitutions at delivery — are each legitimate singly and diagnostic in aggregate: the monthly exceptions read by user, item, and reason shows where the discipline bends, and chronic bending at one till, one gate, or one item is a training or design conversation the read triggers. The principle across all of it is module 1's, applied to identity: the records are testimony, and the audits are how testimony keeps its credibility — cheap, calendared, and boring when everything is fine, which is precisely the state they exist to certify.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Identity in the daily flow
lessons.html:
Identity is not a crisis feature; it is a daily habit, and this chapter walks it through the ordinary day so the crisis chapters stay theoretical.

At the till and the counter. Batch-tracked sales pick a batch at the moment of sale — FEFO offering the earliest, the pick confirmed against the physical carton in hand (the two-second glance at the printed lot that keeps the record true). The friction is real and small; the design answers keep it small: barcodes carrying batch where the trade supports them, the shelf discipline that FEFO's physical layout mirrors the system's suggestion (earliest at the front — the stocker enforces FEFO before the till ever asks), and the till trained that the batch line is custody, not ceremony. Serial sales are rarer and slower by nature (the unit's number confirmed at handover) and the slowness is the product: the customer watches their unit's identity recorded, which is the warranty's first document.

In transfers. Inv 2 gave the rule; identity gives it teeth: dispatches list the batches and serials riding; the receiving branch confirms IDENTITY, not just quantity — 20 cartons arrived, but WHICH lots? The batch-level receipt is minutes and it is the only defence against the swap-en-route (good dating dispatched, short dating arrived, the difference sold out the back — a real pattern, and batch-blind receiving is what makes it invisible). The transit shortfall protocol inherits identity too: what is missing is named by lot, which scopes the loss (and the recall exposure, if the lot ever matters) precisely.

In returns. The identity match is the gate's first question: the returning serial is checked against its delivery (the impossible-return catch — the unit we never sold, the unit sold elsewhere seeking our refund); the returning batch is confirmed against what that customer received (the credit claimed on goods from another source). Matches proceed to triage with biography intact; mismatches become a different conversation, held politely and from documents. The return desk with identity discipline is a fraud filter; without it, a laundry.

In repack and internal movements. The mapping rule from Inv 2, now as daily habit: consumed batches to produced outputs recorded per entry, spot-checked per Chapter 6; write-offs and issues naming their lots always (the biography's ending is a ledger line, not a shrug); and quarantine's contents batch-labelled physically and in record — the bay the recall sweeps first should be the bay that answers fastest.

The habit's economics, told honestly. Identity discipline costs seconds at every gate, till, and truck — a real, recurring, visible cost — and pays in events that are rare, invisible when prevented, and catastrophic when unprevented. Teams do not sustain disciplines they experience as pointless taxation, so the consultant's implementation job is making the payoff visible on ordinary days: the monthly identity page (audit results, exceptions read, FEFO compliance, expiry losses trending down) shown to the team that earned it; the mock recall's time posted like a fire-drill record; the war stories (the swap caught, the impossible return refused) told. The firms whose identity systems still work in year three are the firms where the team can say what the seconds buy.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: the letter arrives at HealthTrade
lessons.html:
The module's threads converge on one Tuesday morning: a NAFDAC letter names batch B-1147 of PARA-500 — a manufacturer-level quality recall, all stock to be quarantined and accounted. The run-book comes off the shelf. Clock: 08:40.

08:40-08:55 — freeze (Ch. 5 step 1). Batch hold applied network-wide; tills at all three sites see the block; the working grid pulled: B-1147 shows 34 cartons at Central, 12 at Ibadan, 0 at Abeokuta (their stock was always B-1152), 0 in transit — and, via the repack mapping, 88 retail strips at Central produced from the lot (Inv 2's entry cited by line). The physical freeze is confirmed by each storekeeper against the grid.

08:55-09:20 — inbound packet (step 2). The receipt that bore B-1147 (Emzor drop one — Procurement 6's case study, now evidence): PO, receipt, quantities, the expiry as captured, Emzor's own lot documentation from the shipment file. The packet goes to the MD for the NAFDAC and Emzor correspondence — twenty-five minutes from letter to a documented inbound story.

09:20-10:30 — holdings verified, outbound traced (steps 3-4). Physical counts confirm the grid (34 + 12 + 88 strips), all moved to quarantine bays, batch-labelled. The outbound trace runs: every DN and sale carrying B-1147 — 118 cartons across six weeks: 74 to four wholesale customers (named, quantified, dated), 44 across branch retail (aggregate, per the trade's nature and the regulator's tiering — retail-level recall handled by point-of-sale notice per the policy). The contact list is real by 10:30.

10:30-12:40 — contact & retrieval begin (step 5). The four wholesale customers notified with their exact quantities and dates (documented); two confirm stock on hand for uplift — the returns will arrive through the gate with batch identity checked (what comes back must BE B-1147). Point-of-sale notices posted per policy. NAFDAC's acknowledgment records the response began same-morning.

12:40 — the reconciliation page (step 6). Received 180 − sold 118 − held 46 (34+12) − repacked-held 16 (the strip equivalent) − written-off 0 = zero unaccounted, per warehouse, every figure a ledger line. Four hours from letter to a page the regulator, the manufacturer, and counsel can each hold. The mock drill run last quarter (3h 50m) predicted the time within minutes — and had already fixed the one gap it found (Ibadan's receiving was confirming quantity but not lot; retrained then, decisive today).

The quiet epilogues (Ch. 4, 6). The same week's serial audit finds one ghost: a chiller serial recorded from a setup-era packing list, never physically present — investigated, written off with its story, and the capture-from-the-unit rule re-taught with a live exhibit. And the expiry horizon, doing its undramatic weekly work, flags B-1152's Ibadan balance entering the 90-day window with velocity too low to clear it: the markdown ladder's first rung (push and front-shelf) executes, and six weeks later the balance clears at full-to-first-rung prices — the write-off that never happened, invisible precisely because the horizon was read. The identity system's year: one crisis passed in four hours, one ghost exorcised, one markdown that saved ₦300k of quiet money — the seconds at the gates, priced.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the third law
lessons.html:
The identity layer's scar tissue — and every disease here shares one anatomy: coverage paid for at the gates and destroyed by a habit. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — the recall that cannot run. Symptom: the letter arrives; the batch's whereabouts are a research project. Disease: capture skipped or faked at the gates (the identity theatre — flags on, discipline off), movements batch-blind, the grid fictional. Fix: painful reconstruction once (supplier documents against sales records — weeks, in the newspapers' shadow), then the gate disciplines with their audits, and the mock recall as the standing certificate that it cannot happen again.

Pattern 2 — FEFO dead by a thousand overrides. Symptom: expiry write-offs climbing while the FEFO flag sits proudly on. Disease: habitual override (Ch. 4) — the front-row grab, the unlogged exception, the fresh batch bleeding out first. Fix: the compliance read by user and reason, the shelf layout that makes FEFO physical, and the ladder worked early so the horizon never becomes a cliff.

Pattern 3 — ghosts in the serial file. Symptom: in-stock serials nobody can produce; impossible sales; audits that will not close. Disease: packing-list capture and duplicate keying (Ch. 2, 6). Fix: capture from the unit as gate law, the periodic serial audit with its three-outcome triage, and ghosts exorcised by documented write-off with the leak that born them named and fixed.

Pattern 4 — the batch-blind branch. Symptom: branch batch records diverge from shelves; the swap-en-route invisible; recall sweeps stall at one site. Disease: quantity-only receiving at transfers (Ch. 7) — identity dying at the network's joints. Fix: batch-level receipt as the transfer gate's rule, the integrity arithmetic (batch sums vs bin actuals) per warehouse monthly, and the mock recall timing each site separately so the weak joint names itself.

Pattern 5 — the merged lot. Symptom: one recorded batch, two physical lots; a recall that must take everything. Disease: ledger mixing for tidiness (Ch. 3). Fix: lots distinct in record without exception, the physical mixing policy decided deliberately (and for pharma, usually prohibited), and the spot-check that compares printed cartons against the recorded mix.

Pattern 6 — identity as decoration. Symptom: the flags are on, the reports unread, the audits never run, the team cannot say what the seconds buy. Disease: coverage without operation — cost with no product (Ch. 1, 7). Fix: either OPERATE it (the monthly identity page, the calendar rhythms, the drill) or, for items where the honest answer is that nobody will ever read it, revisit the architecture decision consciously — a flag removed deliberately beats a discipline performed falsely.

The third law. Module 1: the tree is the map of custody. Module 2: stock moves only by documents. This module: identity is operational, not decorative — a serial or batch captured but never read is cost without coverage, and a discipline read daily makes the crisis drill just Tuesday. Capture from the goods, move by name, receive by lot, pick by expiry, audit on the calendar, and drill the run-book — and the letter, when it comes, is four hours of executing a procedure instead of four weeks of archaeology.

counting.title: Inventory 4 — Stock Reconciliation & Counting
counting.desc: The dialogue between ledger and shelf: the reconciliation document, opening stock at cost, the full count with freeze discipline, the ABC cycle counting programme, variance investigation before adjustment, and shrinkage as a managed number.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Why count: the dialogue
lessons.html:
Three modules built a ledger worth believing. This module tests the belief: the count — the moment the ledger's testimony and the shelf's reality are held against each other, and the differences are made to speak.

The count is a dialogue, not a verdict. The ledger says 96; the shelf says 93. Neither is automatically right: the ledger may have missed a movement (the transfer receipt never entered), the shelf may be hiding stock (the mis-shelved cartons two aisles over), or three units may genuinely be gone. The count's product is not a corrected number — it is the QUESTION, held open long enough to be answered (Chapter 6's investigation discipline), and only then the adjustment, in the open, with its reason. A firm that treats counting as typing shelf numbers over ledger numbers has built an eraser, not a control — and Chapter 9 convicts that eraser by name.

What counting confirms — and what it cannot fix. Where modules 1-3 were kept (movements documented, gates honest, identity captured), the count is a CONFIRMATION: small differences, explainable, adjusted with confidence. Where they were not, the count is a CONFESSION — and the critical understanding is that counting cannot substitute for the disciplines it tests: the firm that counts weekly because its movements are chaos is bailing a boat it refuses to patch; every count resets the water level and the leak remains. Counting frequency is not a virtue by itself; the virtue is a ledger that counting keeps AGREEING with, which is earned upstream.

The three jobs of a counting regime. Accuracy: the operational numbers everyone trades on (the four numbers of every bin) verified on a cadence proportionate to their importance. Accountability: the custodian's number (module 1) made fair — the storekeeper answerable for ₦11m deserves the periodic, documented moment where their custody is confirmed, which protects the honest custodian exactly as much as it exposes the other kind. Deterrence: the counted warehouse steals from itself less — not because counts catch everything, but because the KNOWLEDGE of counting changes behaviour; the cadence's very existence is a control, and irregular, unpredictable elements in the programme (Chapter 5) sharpen it.

The count's own economics. Counting costs hours and interrupts trade, which is why this module spends two chapters on making it cheap: the full count made rare by the cycle programme, the cycle programme weighted by value so effort lands where money sits, and the freeze disciplines that keep a count from being a moving target counted twice. The end state — the well-run firm's relationship with counting — is undramatic by design: small, scheduled, boring counts whose variances are small, explained, and trending nowhere. Boring is the certificate.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Stock Reconciliation document
lessons.html:
The count's instrument is the Stock Reconciliation — the document that records what was counted and writes the ledger entries that make the books agree with the shelves. Its anatomy, and the weight each field carries.

  • Purpose — the document serves two distinct jobs under one roof: Opening Stock (Chapter 3's set piece — loading a warehouse's starting truth at go-live) and the ongoing Stock Reconciliation (the count adjustment). Same machinery, very different governance, and the purpose field says which is happening.
  • Posting date and time — WHEN the count's truth applies. The chronology law at its most sensitive: the reconciliation asserts the counted quantity AS OF this moment, and every ledger read after it builds on that assertion — which is why the count's cutoff discipline (Chapter 4) and the posting timestamp must agree, and why backdated reconciliations are accountant-supervised territory (module 5 walks the valuation ripple they cause).
  • The rows — item, warehouse, counted quantity, and (where the document is also asserting value — opening stock, or a deliberate revaluation) the valuation rate. Submission computes the difference against the ledger's current quantity and writes the adjusting entries: ins for surpluses, outs for shortfalls, valued per the item's costing. The adjustment IS a ledger movement like any other — appended, attributed, dated — which is the append-only law keeping even corrections honest.
  • Identity rows — for batch-tracked items the count is per BATCH (the counted quantity of B-1147 at Ibadan, not just PARA-500 at Ibadan — the integrity arithmetic of module 3 depends on counts feeding it at batch level); for serialized items the reconciliation names serials (which units exist here — the serial audit's formal instrument). A reconciliation that counts identity-tracked items identity-blind repairs the quantity while corrupting the grid beneath it — half a fix that module 3's audits will re-flag.
  • Reason and reference — the count sheet, the variance investigation's outcome, the reason CODE (Chapter 7's aggregation lives on these): the adjustment without a stated reason is the eraser wearing a document's clothes.

What submission does — and its blast radius. The adjusting entries change actual quantities, therefore projected quantities, therefore everything that reads them: availability promises, reorder triggers, valuations. A large reconciliation is a large event — reviewed before submission (the two-eyes threshold, by value of adjustment, exactly as write-offs and Material Receipts earned), and timed deliberately (the mid-trading-day reconciliation of a busy warehouse fights its own moving target; Chapter 4's windows exist for this). Draft, verify against the signed count records, check identity rows, check the rate columns are doing what you intend — the rate column on an ordinary count adjustment should usually assert nothing (quantity correction at existing valuation), and a rate typed carelessly there is a revaluation nobody meant to perform. Then submit, and the dialogue's answer becomes the ledger's next line.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Opening stock done right: the at-cost law
lessons.html:
Every implementation has one moment where years of a client's stock truth are keyed into a new system in a week — and one mistake at that moment poisons every number the system will ever produce. This chapter is the set piece: go-live opening stock, and the conviction that headlines it.

The sequence. Opening stock is loaded by Stock Reconciliation (purpose: Opening Stock), warehouse by warehouse, and the sequence is not negotiable: count first, then load — the physical count of what actually exists at cutover, not the old system's report (the old system's errors are precisely what the fresh start should shed, and loading its numbers uncounted imports every ghost it accumulated), and not memory. The count runs with Chapter 4's disciplines (teams, sheets, verification) because it IS a full count — the most important one the firm will ever do, since every future count dialogues against the truth established here.

THE AT-COST LAW. Opening stock enters at cost — the item's honest acquisition cost — never at selling price. This error is common enough, and catastrophic enough, to deserve its own wall: the client's team, keying under deadline, reaches for the price everyone knows (the shelf price, the price list) instead of the cost fewer people know — and the consequences cascade: the stock ASSET inflates by the entire embedded margin (a ₦30m inventory at cost booked as ₦42m at retail is a ₦12m fiction on the balance sheet); COGS inflates the moment selling begins (goods costed at selling price produce ZERO margin on paper — the firm sells briskly for months while reports insist it earns nothing); the distortion cannot be waved away, because valuation flows entry by entry (module 5) and every sale, transfer, and report inherits the poisoned rates until a supervised revaluation exercise — weeks of accountant-led correction — cleans what one week of care would have prevented. When a go-live's first-quarter margins look inexplicably terrible, this is the FIRST suspect, and the consultant who checks the opening rates against purchase records in hour one has usually found it.

Sourcing honest costs. The rate column per item, filled from evidence: recent purchase invoices (the best source — last honest buy, landed where imports apply), the supplier's current lists where purchases are stale, and for the tail with no clean evidence, a defensible estimate DOCUMENTED as such with the accountant's sign-off. The discipline is proportionate: the A-value items (where the money sits) get invoice-level sourcing; the long tail gets a sensible method applied consistently. What no item gets: the selling price, zero (the opposite distortion — module 2's conviction), or a guess nobody wrote down.

Identity at opening. Batch-tracked stock opens per batch WITH expiries — the counting team reads cartons, not just counts them, because an opening that loads PARA-500 as 400 units batch-blind has destroyed FEFO, the horizon, and the recall for every unit of that opening stock forever (the provenance cannot be invented later — module 3's retrofit warning at its sharpest). Serialized stock opens serial by serial from the physical units. Yes, this makes opening slower; it is the identity architecture's admission price, paid once, and the alternative is an identity system that begins life already broken.

The opening file. Count sheets signed, rate sources referenced, the accountant's sign-off on method, the reconciliation documents themselves: the go-live's evidence bundle, filed. The balance sheet's stock figure was BORN here, and the auditor's first question at year one — how was opening stock established? — is answered from this file in minutes or from archaeology in weeks.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The full count: freeze, count, verify
lessons.html:
The wall-to-wall count — annual for most firms, plus the opening set piece — is a production, and productions succeed on planning. The run-book:

Plan. Date chosen against trade (the quiet season, the weekend, the overnight); scope declared (which warehouses, all items); teams assigned in PAIRS with areas mapped (no aisle counted by its own daily custodian ALONE — the second pair of eyes is the accountability design, not an insult); count sheets or devices prepared — and the sheets are blind: the counter records what they SEE, without the ledger's expectation printed beside it, because a sheet showing expected 96 harvests 96 (the anchoring is human and universal; blindness is the cheap cure and Chapter 9's count-theatre conviction is its violation).

Freeze. The count's enemy is movement: stock counted at 10:00 and moved at 10:30 is counted wrong somewhere. The clean solution is the freeze window — no movements in the counted warehouse during the count: receiving paused (trucks scheduled around it), issues and transfers held, sales stopped or (where trade cannot stop) strictly cut over: a hard timestamp, everything before it posted, everything after it segregated and excluded — physically set aside, documented, counted into the NEXT period's truth. The freeze is announced, short, and absolute; a leaky freeze produces variances that are artifacts of the leak, and the investigation chapter's first question about any surprising variance is always did the freeze hold?

Count. Pairs count their areas: physical units, honest UOMs (the carton-and-loose-units discipline — 47 cartons and 6 singles recorded as exactly that, the conversion arithmetic done by the system not the counter's head), identity read where tracked (batches from printed lots WITH quantities per lot; serials sighted). Completed sheets signed by the pair and surrendered — not corrected in the aisle, not reconciled on the fly.

Recount and verify. Entries keyed (or synced) against the ledger; the variance list emerges; and the discipline that separates professionals: material variances are RECOUNTED before they are believed — a second, different pair to the same location, because the largest single source of count variances is the count itself (the missed shelf, the double-counted pallet, the UOM slip). Only variances that survive recount graduate to Chapter 6's investigation. Thresholds make this proportionate: kobo-level noise adjusts without ceremony; value and percentage lines route to recount; the biggest items get counted twice by design regardless.

Close. The reconciliation document(s) drafted from verified counts, reviewed against thresholds, submitted with the count file referenced (sheets, recounts, investigation notes); the freeze lifted; the segregated cutover stock processed into the new period. Sign-offs: the count lead, the custodian (who is confirming their own custody's verdict — the fairness ritual), and finance above the value line. The whole production, well run, is one long day and a filed bundle; badly run, it is a weekend that generates more errors than it finds — and the difference is entirely this run-book.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Cycle counting: the programme
lessons.html:
The annual count is a storm; the cycle counting programme is weather — small counts, continuously, tuned so every item is verified on a cadence its value deserves. This is the counting regime a serious multi-branch firm actually lives on.

The ABC engine. Stock stratified by value-velocity (the analysis module 7 formalises; the programme consumes it): A items — the vital few holding most of the money — counted frequently (monthly is a working default); B items quarterly; C items — the trivial many — annually, effectively riding the full count. The arithmetic that sells the programme: a few lines counted per day per warehouse, fifteen minutes, covers the entire A-class monthly — the effort lands where the money sits, and the annual count shrinks from a discovery expedition to a formality, because everything valuable was verified eleven times since the last one.

The schedule's craft. Published rhythm, unpublished selection: the team knows counts happen daily; WHICH lines today is not posted in advance (predictable counts are gameable counts — the deterrence job needs the element of surprise), and the selection mixes the scheduled cadence with triggers: items with recent variances (re-verified sooner — a variance is a question about a location, and the follow-up count is the answer's confirmation), items touched by incident (the transit shortfall's item, the return desk's disputed line), negative-stock flags (module 5's alarm — counted the day they appear), and a random seasoning. Identity audits ride the same visits (module 3's serial sightings and batch spot-checks appended to the day's lines — one trip, two verifications).

Mechanics in miniature. Each cycle count is the full count's disciplines at teaspoon scale: blind, counted by someone other than the line's daily handler where the roster allows, material variances recounted, survivors investigated (Chapter 6), adjustments reason-coded (Chapter 7). No freeze is needed for a two-line count — the cutover discipline is simply counting at a quiet moment and posting the reconciliation with an honest timestamp — which is exactly why the cycle programme scales where the full count cannot: it never fights the trading day.

The programme's outputs. Beyond corrected bins: the count accuracy rate (lines counted clean ÷ lines counted — the warehouse's ongoing grade, trended per warehouse and per class), the variance pipeline feeding Chapter 7's shrinkage read with fresh, small, investigable differences instead of an annual heap, and the accountability rhythm — every custodian's areas verified continuously, which is the fairness design running on autopilot. A firm with a healthy cycle programme knows its accuracy this month, its shrinkage this quarter, and faces its auditor with a counting FILE instead of a counting weekend.

Right-sizing. The eleven-person single-site firm runs the same idea smaller: a page of A items counted weekly by rotation, the annual full count, the same blindness and recount rules. The programme is a shape, not a headcount — and the consultant's deliverable is the shape sized to the client: the strata, the cadences, the daily line quota, the trigger list, and the named owner of the schedule.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Variance investigation: before you adjust
lessons.html:
A variance that survives recount is a fact: the ledger and the shelf disagree, and the disagreement is real. The amateur move is adjusting it away; the professional move is this chapter — the investigation that makes the adjustment TRUE instead of merely tidy.

Why investigate first. The adjustment writes history (the append-only ledger accepts it forever) and closes the question — and a question closed wrong stays wrong twice: the root cause survives to generate next month's variance, and the adjustment itself may be backwards (the shortage adjusted away at warehouse A that was really a surplus mis-shelved at warehouse B now becomes TWO wrong bins made permanent). The investigation window — variances held open, worked, and only then adjusted — is the discipline; its length is policy (days, not weeks: an aging variance list is its own disease), and its output is a CAUSE attached to every material adjustment.

The taxonomy — where differences actually come from, in rough order of frequency:

  • Unposted or mis-posted documents — the transfer dispatched but never received (the goods sit in transit; the branch counted short against a bin that never received them), the delivery picked but the DN unsubmitted, the receipt keyed to the wrong date. The ledger walk (module 1's diagnostic) finds these in minutes: the item's recent entries against the physical paper trail, and the fix is POSTING the missing truth, not adjusting around it — an adjustment that papers over an unposted document creates a double error the day the document finally posts.
  • Wrong-warehouse postings — the mirror shortage-and-surplus pair (module 1's disease): warehouse A short exactly what warehouse B is over. The cross-check is cheap (the same item's variances across warehouses, netted) and the fix is the correcting transfer, not two adjustments.
  • UOM errors — the factor-of-twelve signatures: variances at suspicious ratios (short 110 on a Carton-12 item is one mis-keyed carton row, not 110 missing units). The conversion arithmetic checked before the loss is believed.
  • Identity drift — quantity right, batches wrong (module 3's orphans): not a stock adjustment at all, but a batch correction with its own discipline.
  • Count error residue — the recount missed something too; a third look at stubborn variances before the expensive conclusions.
  • Genuine loss — what remains when the ledger walk, the cross-checks, and the recounts all hold: damage unrecorded, theft, leakage. Now — and only now — the adjustment, reason-coded as loss, feeding the shrinkage read, and (by value and pattern) the escalation the firm's policy names: the custody conversation, the security review, the incident file.

The investigation's own file. Material variances carry their working: what was checked, what was found, who concluded. Thirty lines of notes that turn the adjustment from an assertion into a finding — the difference an auditor, an insurer, or a dismissal hearing will care about intensely. And the aggregate of causes (Chapter 7) is management information of the first order: a warehouse whose variances are 80% unposted documents has a discipline problem with a training fix; one whose variances are unexplained loss has a different problem with a different fix — and only investigation, done every time, can tell the two apart.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Shrinkage: the managed number
lessons.html:
Every investigated variance ends as a reason-coded adjustment, and the codes aggregate into the number this chapter is about: shrinkage — the value of stock the firm lost, stated, trended, and managed like any other cost of trading.

The read. Adjustments-as-loss, aggregated: by period (the trend line), by warehouse (the custody comparison), by category (where the leakage concentrates — the pilferable smalls vs the bulky staples), by cause code (process failures vs damage vs unexplained). Expressed as a RATE — shrinkage value against throughput or holding value — because the raw naira grows with the business and the rate is the honest comparator: quarter on quarter, warehouse against warehouse, the firm against its trade's rough benchmarks. The read exists the moment reason codes are used consistently, which is why Chapter 6 insisted on them: shrinkage is not a special report; it is the investigation discipline's exhaust, collected.

Reading it like management. The rate's LEVEL sets the response scale (a fraction of a percent is the cost of doing business managed well; multiples of it are a program, not a number); the TREND is the alarm (a stable 0.4% is peace; 0.4% becoming 0.9% in two quarters is a change with a cause — new staff? new category? a control that lapsed?); the DISTRIBUTION is the map (one branch at triple the network rate is a located problem — custody, security, or discipline, and the branch comparison is what locates it); and the CAUSE MIX is the prescription: process-heavy shrinkage (unposted, mis-posted, UOM) is fixed by training and the earlier modules' disciplines; damage-heavy by handling and storage; unexplained-heavy by the harder conversations — access control, the counting programme's unpredictability turned up, and where pattern warrants, the investigation the firm's policy and the law provide for. The consultant's framing for owners: you cannot price, insure, or staff against a number you refuse to know — and the firms shocked annually by stocktake write-offs are not unlucky; they are unread.

The deterrence dividend. The read's existence changes the number it reads: custodians who know shrinkage is computed per custody, counts arrive unpredictably, and variances get investigated (not just adjusted) work in a different atmosphere — the honest are protected by the same machinery that exposes the other kind, which is module 1's custodian framing paying its dividend. The atmosphere is the cheapest control in this entire module, and it is built from nothing but consistency: counts that happen, investigations that conclude, and a number that someone visibly reads.

What shrinkage is not. Not a bucket for lazy differences (the uninvestigated variance coded unexplained is a lie with a category), not a write-off holiday (the quarterly shrinkage posting does not replace item-level, reason-coded adjustments — aggregation without granularity manages nothing), and not shameful to report (the owner who wants shrinkage hidden from the monthly pack is asking to be surprised annually instead — the number's job is to be seen small and often). The mature end state: shrinkage on the monthly management page beside consumables and write-offs, boring, small, and watched — the warehouse's cost of reality, priced.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's counting year
lessons.html:
The counting regime, lived for a year. Every chapter clocks in.

The go-live opening (Ch. 3). Cutover weekend: full count first — pairs, blind sheets, batches read from cartons with expiries, the chiller serials sighted. Then the load... and the near-miss that justifies the module: the draft opening reconciliation, keyed by the client's team from their price list because those were the numbers we had, shows Central's stock at ₦61m. The consultant's hour-one check — opening rates against recent purchase invoices — catches it: the rates are SELLING prices. Re-sourced at cost (invoice-level for the A items, documented method for the tail, accountant's sign-off), the honest figure is ₦42m. The ₦19m phantom dies in Draft — the balance sheet never carries it, the margins never lie, and the client's accountant becomes the implementation's loudest advocate. The opening file closes: sheets, sources, sign-offs, documents.

The programme designed (Ch. 5). ABC run on the opening data: 62 A items (71% of value), counted monthly — five lines per day per warehouse, fifteen minutes; B quarterly; C rides the annual. Selection unpublished; triggers wired (variance follow-ups, incident items, negative-stock flags — plus module 3's identity audits riding the visits). The schedule has an owner, and the first month's count accuracy posts at 96.8%.

The investigation (Ch. 6). Month three, a cycle count finds Ibadan short 8 cartons of amoxicillin — survives recount. The investigation window opens: the ledger walk shows a transfer dispatched from Central twelve days prior... and never received — the goods sat in In-Transit the whole time (module 2's aging read had flagged the room that same morning; the two diagnostics converge on one truth). Physical check: the cartons are AT Ibadan — arrived, shelved, receipt never entered by a leave-covering stand-in. The fix is the missing POSTING (the transfer receipt, entered with its honest story), not an adjustment — which would have created the double error the day anyone found the paperwork. Cause coded: unposted document; the stand-in trained; the variance list closes at zero adjustment. The system worked BECAUSE nobody reached for the eraser.

The full count (Ch. 4). Year-end, one Sunday: freeze announced and absolute (trucks rescheduled, tills dark 06:00-14:00), pairs on mapped areas, blind sheets, material variances recounted by fresh pairs. The verified list is short — the cycle programme spent a year keeping it short — and the biggest surviving item is a UOM signature (short exactly 24 on a Carton-12 line: two carton rows keyed as units at a February cycle count, corrected with the conversion checked). Sign-offs: count lead, each custodian, finance. One day, one file, no drama.

The shrinkage read (Ch. 7). Four quarters posted: 0.42%, 0.38%, 0.44%, 0.41% — stable, small, cause-mix dominated by damage and process residue, unexplained under a third of the total and flat. One distribution flag mid-year: Abeokuta's Q2 rate at double the network — investigated (a rear-door access pattern, resolved with a lock policy and two months of trigger counts), back on-trend by Q3. The number lived on the monthly page all year; nobody was surprised in December. Boring — which was the point, and the certificate.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the fourth law
lessons.html:
The counting layer's scar tissue. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — the reconciliation as eraser. Symptom: variances adjusted same-day, uninvestigated; the same lines varying every count. Disease: the question closed without being answered (Ch. 1, 6) — root causes immortal, wrong-way adjustments compounding. Fix: the investigation window as unskippable routine, causes coded on every material adjustment, and the follow-up count that verifies the answer held.

Pattern 2 — opening at selling price. Symptom: inflated stock asset; first-quarter margins near zero while trade is brisk. Disease: the at-cost law broken at the one moment it cannot be cheaply unbroken (Ch. 3). Fix: caught in Draft — the hour-one check of opening rates against purchase records; caught late — the supervised revaluation exercise with the accountant, weeks of it, and the lesson institutionalised.

Pattern 3 — counting a moving target. Symptom: variances that vanish on recount; count weekends that generate more errors than they find. Disease: the freeze leaked (Ch. 4) — movements mid-count making every sheet a snapshot of a different moment. Fix: the freeze window absolute or the cutover strict; the first investigation question, always: did the freeze hold?

Pattern 4 — effort inverted. Symptom: the trivial tail counted obsessively while A items drift for quarters. Disease: the programme unweighted (Ch. 5) — effort spread by item count instead of value. Fix: the ABC engine, the daily quota landing on the vital few, and the accuracy rate reported per class so the inversion is visible.

Pattern 5 — count theatre. Symptom: sheets that match the ledger perfectly, always. Disease: counting from the screen (Ch. 4) — expectations printed, aisles skipped, the blindness rule dead and with it the entire exercise. Fix: blind sheets structurally, pairs and rotation, spot re-counts of counted areas by the schedule owner — and the accuracy rate treated with suspicion when it is TOO perfect.

Pattern 6 — the unread number. Symptom: adjustments posted for years; nobody can state the shrinkage rate. Disease: the exhaust never collected (Ch. 7) — reason codes inconsistent or absent, the annual shock arriving on schedule. Fix: the code list short and enforced, the quarterly read on the management page, and the trend owned by a name.

The fourth law. Module 1: the tree is the map of custody. Module 2: stock moves only by documents. Module 3: identity is operational. This module: the count is a dialogue between the ledger and the shelf — investigate before you adjust, and adjust in the open. Open at cost, count blind, freeze honestly, recount before believing, name every cause, and read the number the causes add up to. A firm that keeps this law faces auditors with files, custodians with fairness, and December with boredom — and its ledger, tested continuously and found truthful, becomes the asset the next module prices: valuation, where every quantity this module verified meets the money it represents.

opts: Destroys FEFO, the horizon, and the recall for that stock forever — provenance cannot be invented later
questions.why: The identity architecture's admission price, paid once.

questions.q: Count sheets are blind because:
opts: A sheet showing expected 96 harvests 96 — anchoring is human and universal
questions.why: Blindness is the cheap cure.

questions.q: The freeze exists because:
opts: Stock counted at 10:00 and moved at 10:30 is counted wrong somewhere
questions.why: Absolute window, or strict cutover with segregation.

questions.q: Material variances are recounted before belief because:
opts: The largest single source of count variances is the count itself
questions.why: The missed shelf, the double-counted pallet, the UOM slip.

questions.q: No aisle is counted by its daily custodian ALONE because:
opts: The second pair of eyes is the accountability design — protecting the honest custodian too
questions.why: Fairness and control in one rule.

questions.q: The ABC engine counts:
opts: A items monthly, B quarterly, C annually — effort landing where the money sits
questions.why: Fifteen minutes a day covers the A-class monthly.

questions.q: Count selection is unpublished because:
opts: Predictable counts are gameable counts — deterrence needs surprise
questions.why: Published rhythm, unpublished lines, plus triggers and random seasoning.

questions.q: Cycle count triggers include:
opts: Recent variances, incident items, negative-stock flags — plus identity audits riding the visits
questions.why: One trip, two verifications.

questions.q: The count accuracy rate is:
opts: Lines counted clean over lines counted — the warehouse's ongoing grade, trended
questions.why: And treated with suspicion when TOO perfect.

questions.q: Adjusting before investigating risks:
opts: Immortal root causes and backwards adjustments — two wrong bins made permanent
questions.why: A question closed wrong stays wrong twice.

questions.q: The most frequent variance cause is:
opts: Unposted or mis-posted documents — found by the ledger walk in minutes
questions.why: The fix is POSTING the missing truth, never adjusting around it.

questions.q: Warehouse A short exactly what B is over signals:
opts: A wrong-warehouse posting — fixed by a correcting transfer, not two adjustments
questions.why: The mirror pair, netted cheaply.

questions.q: A variance of exactly 110 on a Carton-12 item suggests:
opts: A UOM signature — one mis-keyed carton row; check the arithmetic before believing the loss
questions.why: The factor-of-twelve leaves fingerprints.

questions.q: An adjustment papering over an unposted document:
opts: Creates a double error the day the document finally posts
questions.why: The case study's investigation refused exactly this.

questions.q: Shrinkage is expressed as a RATE because:
opts: The raw naira grows with the business — the rate is the honest comparator
questions.why: Quarter on quarter, warehouse against warehouse.

questions.q: A stable 0.4% becoming 0.9% in two quarters is:
opts: A change with a cause — the trend is the alarm, not the level alone
questions.why: New staff, new category, or a lapsed control.

questions.q: One branch at triple the network shrinkage rate is:
opts: A located problem — the distribution is the map
questions.why: Custody, security, or discipline — and now you know where.

questions.q: Process-heavy vs unexplained-heavy cause mixes prescribe:
opts: Training and discipline vs access control and harder conversations — only investigation tells them apart
questions.why: The cause mix is the prescription.

questions.q: The uninvestigated variance coded 'unexplained' is:
opts: A lie with a category — shrinkage is not a bucket for lazy differences
questions.why: Aggregation without granularity manages nothing.

questions.q: In the case study, the ₦19m phantom was:
opts: Caught in Draft by the hour-one check of opening rates against purchase invoices
questions.why: ₦61m at selling prices became ₦42m at cost before the books ever carried it.

questions.q: The Ibadan amoxicillin variance resolved as:
opts: An unposted transfer receipt — the missing POSTING entered, zero adjustment, stand-in trained
questions.why: Two diagnostics (cycle count and transit aging) converged on one truth.

questions.q: The year-end full count was short and calm because:
opts: The cycle programme spent a year keeping the variance list short
questions.why: The annual count shrank to a formality.

questions.q: Abeokuta's Q2 shrinkage spike was:
opts: Located by the distribution read, investigated, resolved with a lock policy and trigger counts
questions.why: Back on-trend by Q3; nobody surprised in December.

questions.q: Count theatre is detected by:
opts: Suspicion of too-perfect accuracy, blind sheets structurally, spot re-counts by the schedule owner
questions.why: Sheets that always match the ledger are counting the screen.

questions.q: The first investigation question for any surprising full-count variance is:
questions.why: A leaky freeze manufactures variances that are artifacts.

questions.q: This module's law is:
opts: The count is a dialogue between the ledger and the shelf — investigate before you adjust, and adjust in the open
questions.why: Open at cost, count blind, freeze honestly, name every cause, read the number.
